q1.scenario: Pot $100, opponent bets $50, you have a flush draw (9 outs). Flop dealt, two cards to come.
q1.question: Do the pot odds support a call?

optA.explanation: Pot odds = 50/(100+50+50) = 25%. Flush draw post-flop equity ≈ 35% (9 outs × 4). 35% > 25%, calling is +EV.

optB.explanation: The odds are sufficient — don't fold. A flush draw has ~35% equity post-flop, well above the required 25%.

q2.question: Approximately how many outs do you have?

optA.explanation: You not only have a straight draw but also a flush draw.

optB.explanation: You not only have a flush draw but also a straight draw.

optC.explanation: Flush 9 outs + open-ended straight 8 outs - overlap ~2 = about 15 outs. A strong combo draw with ~54% equity.

optD.explanation: Your draw is far stronger than a gutshot — you have a flush + open-ended straight combo draw.

q3.scenario: Pot $20, opponent bets $15. You hold a small pocket pair (set mining). Effective stack $200.
q3.question: Direct pot odds don't justify a call, but what about implied odds?

optA.explanation: Direct odds = 15/(20+15+15) = 30%, set mining at ~12% isn't enough. But implied odds: hitting a set can win more from villain; effective stack/call = 200/15 ≈ 13:1, well above the required ~7.5:1.

optB.explanation: This ignores implied odds with deep stacks. Set mining deep-stacked is a classic implied odds play.

q4.scenario: You hold K♠Q♠, flop is K♥7♦3♣. Villain bets large on a wet board.
q4.question: What problem might you face here?

optA.text: Reverse implied odds — top pair may be dominated
optA.explanation: KQ hit top pair but the kicker isn't the strongest. If villain holds AK or KK, the more you invest the more you lose. A classic reverse implied odds spot.

optB.text: No risk, top pair is strong
optB.explanation: KQ's kicker isn't the best (AK dominates you). A large bet suggests a strong range — be wary.

q5.scenario: Pot $80, opponent bets $80 (full pot). You have an open-ended straight draw (8 outs), Turn dealt, one card to come.
q5.question: Should you call?

optA.explanation: 8 outs after the turn has only ~17% equity. Required odds = 80/(80+80+80) = 33%. 17% < 33%, direct odds aren't enough.

optB.explanation: Pot odds require 33%, but 8 outs after the turn is ~17% (8×2+1). Unless huge implied odds exist, fold.

q6.scenario: You hold A♥K♥, flop is 2♥7♥9♣. You have the nut flush draw + two overcards.
q6.question: Approximately how many outs do you have?

optA.explanation: Don't forget your two overcards (A and K) can also pair up.

optB.explanation: Flush 9 outs + overcard pair 6 outs (3 As + 3 Ks) = 15 outs. A very strong draw with ~54% equity.

optC.explanation: You also have the nut flush draw — far more than overcard outs.

q7.scenario: Pot $60, opponent bets $20 (1/3 pot). You have a gutshot draw (4 outs), Flop dealt.
q7.question: Do the pot odds support a call?

optA.text: Yes, the small bet gives good odds
optA.explanation: Pot odds = 20/(60+20+20) = 20%. Gutshot post-flop equity ≈ 16% (4×4). Close, but with implied odds (hitting a straight can win more), a call is reasonable.

optB.explanation: Only 4 outs, but villain gives a great price (only 20% equity needed). With implied odds, calling is +EV.

q8.scenario: You hold 5♦5♣, UTG opens to $15, effective stack $300. You're on BTN.
q8.question: Is set mining profitable here?

optA.text: Yes, deep-stack implied odds are excellent
optA.explanation: Set mining needs about 15-20× the call amount in implied chips. $300/$15 = 20×, satisfying the condition. Hitting a set will likely win a big pot.

optB.text: No, pocket pair is too weak
optB.explanation: Set mining a small pocket pair deep-stacked is a classic profitable play — 20× implied odds is enough.

q9.scenario: You hold A♣T♣, flop is A♦8♣5♠. Villain check-raises your bet.
q9.question: Why be careful here?

optA.text: Reverse implied odds: AT's top pair is dominated by stronger Ax
optA.explanation: A check-raise usually means strength. Villain may have AK, AQ, AJ, or a set. Your AT top pair with a mediocre kicker faces serious reverse implied odds — win small, lose big.

optB.text: Top pair top kicker, should shove
optB.explanation: AT is not top pair top kicker (AK/AQ/AJ dominate you). Be cautious against a check-raise.

q10.scenario: Pot $200, opponent shoves $100. You have a flush + gutshot combo draw (~12 outs), Turn dealt.
q10.question: Should you call?

optA.explanation: Pot odds = 100/(200+100+100) = 25%. 12 outs after the turn ≈ 24% (12×2). Very close, plus possible backdoor chances — a call is roughly break-even to slightly profitable.

optB.explanation: 12 outs ≈ 24% is very close to the required 25%. With possible extra outs and precise calculation, this is a marginal call.

q11.scenario: You hold J♠T♠, flop is Q♠9♠3♦. You have a flush draw + open-ended straight draw.
q11.question: After accounting for overlap, how many effective outs?

optA.explanation: You can't just add 9+8=17 — there's overlap (e.g., K♠ and 8♠ complete both the flush and the straight).

optB.explanation: Flush 9 + straight 8 - overlap 2 (K♠ and 8♠) = 15 effective outs. A very strong combo draw.

optC.explanation: You also have flush draw outs — far more than 8.

optD.explanation: You also have open-ended straight outs — far more than 9.

q12.scenario: You hold 7♣6♣, villain opens CO to $10. Effective stack $80. You're in BB.
q12.question: Are the implied odds for set mining / speculative calls enough?

optA.explanation: Implied odds need ~15-20×: $80/$10 = 8×, well below required. Suited-connector speculation is hard to profit shallow — fold or 3-bet.

optB.text: Yes, speculative hands always win big pots
optB.explanation: 8× implied odds is far from enough. You need at least 15× to make speculative calls profitable.

q13.scenario: Pot $150, opponent bets $37.5 (1/4 pot). You have the nut flush draw (9 outs), Flop dealt.
q13.question: Facing this small bet, you should?

optA.explanation: Pot odds = 37.5/(150+37.5+37.5) = 16.7%. Flush draw post-flop ≈ 35% equity. 35% >> 16.7% — an excellent call. Raising can even be considered.

optB.explanation: Regardless of villain's hand, you only need 16.7% equity to call and you have 35%. Mathematically you must call.

q14.scenario: You hold A♠J♠, flop is A♥T♦4♣. Villain c-bets, you call. Turn is 2♣, villain bets large again.
q14.question: What do two consecutive large bets suggest?

optA.text: Reverse implied odds increase: villain may have AK/AQ/two pair/set
optA.explanation: Two consecutive large bets (double barrel) usually represent a strong range. AJ top pair with a mediocre kicker faces serious reverse implied odds — you win when villain is weak, lose when villain is strong.

optB.explanation: Could be a bluff, but large bets on two streets are more often value. AJ is a typical bluff-catcher here, but reverse implied odds risk is high.

q15.scenario: Pot $40, opponent overbets $120 (3× pot). You have a gutshot (4 outs), Turn dealt, one card to come.
q15.question: Should you call?

optA.text: Call, hitting the straight wins a big pot
optA.explanation: Required equity = 120/(40+120+120) = 42.9%, but 4 outs after the turn is only ~8.7% (4/46, Rule of 2 ≈ 4×2=8%). Huge gap — "hitting wins big" cannot bridge 34 percentage points.

optB.explanation: Required equity = 120/(40+120+120) = 42.9%. A gutshot after the turn has only ~8.7% equity (4/46). The overbet prices draws out completely — a clear fold.

q16.scenario: River, pot $100, opponent bets $100 (full pot). You only have third pair, no draws, can only beat bluffs. Estimated bluff frequency ~20% from the line.
q16.question: By pot odds, should you bluff-catch this river bet?

optA.explanation: Required equity = 100/(100+100+100) = 33.3%. You can only beat bluffs, equity ≈ villain's bluff frequency 20%. 20% < 33.3%, calling is -EV: EV = 0.2×$200 - 0.8×$100 = -$40 — fold.

optB.text: Call, can't let villain push you around
optB.explanation: "Not wanting to be bluffed" isn't a mathematical reason. On the river there's no more action — your equity is villain's bluff frequency 20%, below the required 33.3%. Calling long-term loses.

q17.scenario: Pot $50, opponent bets $50, leaving only $20 behind. You have a flush draw (9 outs), Flop dealt, this call sees only the Turn.
q17.question: Direct odds aren't enough — can implied odds save this call?

optA.text: Yes, the flush draw is worth chasing
optA.explanation: Implied odds are capped by villain's remaining stack. Break-even needs ~$113 more after hitting (50/0.19 ≈ 263, 263-150 = 113), but villain only has $20 — the gap can't be bridged.

optB.explanation: Direct odds = 50/(50+50+50) = 33.3%, one-card equity ≈ 19% (9/47). Break-even needs ~$113 more after hitting (50/0.19 ≈ 263 minus current pot 150), but villain only has $20. Implied odds are capped — fold.

q18.scenario: You hold 6♥5♥, flop is K♥9♥9♣ (paired board). Pot $60, opponent bets $60 (full pot).
q18.question: Should you continue with your low flush draw?

optA.explanation: Nominal 9 outs × 4 ≈ 36% looks enough vs 33.3%, but on a paired board some outs are "dirty": if villain holds 9x/K9, you make a flush while he makes a boat; your 6-high flush can also be dominated by bigger hearts. Effective equity needs heavy discounting.

optB.text: Fold, reverse implied odds too bad
optB.explanation: Required equity = 60/(60+60+60) = 33.3%. Nominal 9 outs (~36%) must be discounted on the paired board: making your flush can still lose to a boat (villain with 9x/K9), and a 6-high flush can be dominated. Effective ~6 outs (~24%), below required — fold.

q19.scenario: Pot $60, a very tight rock-type player bets $60 (full pot). You have a gutshot (4 outs), Flop dealt, this call sees only the Turn.
q19.question: Is chasing a gutshot on implied odds viable?

optA.explanation: Direct odds = 60/(60+60+60) = 33.3%, one-card equity ≈ 8.5% (4/47). Break-even needs ~$526 more after hitting (60/0.085 ≈ 706 minus current pot 180), and rock-type players almost never pay big on obvious scary boards. The implied odds are an illusion — fold.

optB.text: Yes, the gutshot is disguised and wins big when it hits
optB.explanation: "Disguised" doesn't mean "gets paid". The gap needs ~$526 more after hitting to break even, and a super-tight villain won't pay that size. Be extra conservative about implied odds vs tight players.

easy.scenario: Pot 100, opponent checks (bets 0). You call 0 to see the next card.
easy.question: Is calling profitable here?

optA.text: Yes, a free card is always profitable
optA.explanation: Call amount is 0, required equity = 0/(100+0+0) = 0%. Every hand satisfies it — calling (effectively checking) is always +EV.

optB.explanation: Calling 0 needs no equity; folding gives up a free card.
